justification:
Ran `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/csharp-dotnet/generics.md` three times from Git Bash: PASS, blocks=20, executed=14, identical every time (deterministic — no timing-only blocks besides the wildcarded box-cost lines).

**All six compiler diagnostics independently reproduced from scratch**, in my own throwaway file-based programs (`dotnet run <file>.cs`, same mechanism run-code.mjs uses), not copy-pasted from the article: CS1503 ('Argument 1: cannot convert from 'string' to 'int''), CS0452 ('The type 'int' must be a reference type in order to use it as parameter 'T'...'), CS0453 ('The type 'string' must be a non-nullable value type...'), CS0310 (''Monster' must be a non-abstract type with a public parameterless constructor...'), CS0029 ('Cannot implicitly convert type 'List<Circle>' to 'List<Shape>''), and both CS1961s ('the type parameter 'T' must be contravariantly valid on 'IProducer<T>.Accept(T)'. 'T' is covariant.' and the mirrored 'must be covariantly valid on 'IConsumer<T>.Get()'. 'T' is contravariant.'). Every diagnostic and message text the article shows or quotes matches what the compiler actually emitted for me, verbatim.

**Reification independently verified.** My own standalone version of the `typeof(T)`/`GetType()` block produced byte-identical output to the article's: `System.Collections.Generic.List\`1[System.Int32]`, `...[System.String]`, `True`, and `T is System.Int32`/`System.String here, not just object` for the two `Describe<T>` calls. `ids.GetType() == typeof(List<int>)` is `True` because closed generic types are canonicalized/cached per type argument at the CLR level — the article's identity claim holds.

**Boxing-cost benchmark independently verified.** My own copy of the `box-cost` block, run three times, gave the exact same total both lists (`31999996000000`, which is the correct closed form n(n-1)/2 for n=8,000,000) every time, and the boxed `ArrayList` loop was consistently ~6-8x slower than the typed `List<int>` loop (e.g. 32-34 ms vs 4-6 ms) across all three runs — consistent with the article's wildcarded, qualitative 'several times slower... never close' framing, which correctly does not pin an exact multiple.

**Sourcing checked against fetched primary text.** All eight front-matter sources are cited inline (no uncited-source finding, unlike the pilot lesson flagged elsewhere). Every quoted fragment — the two 'Generic types and methods' quotes, the 'Generics in .NET' boxing-performance bullet, all three Oracle type-erasure steps, and the `INumberBase<TSelf>.Zero` signature — came back character-for-character exact against the fetched pages. The unquoted, paraphrased claims (new() must be last; IEnumerable<T>/IComparer<T> variance; every built-in numeric type implements INumber<T>) are all substantively supported by the pages cited for them.

**Honesty disclaimers checked and present.** The Java-erasure section explicitly says the C#/Java contrast 'is Java's documented design, not a limitation this page tested against a running JVM' — present, and accurate: nothing in the article claims to have run Java code. Separately, I searched the full article text for any mention of JIT specialization/monomorphization (the CLR's per-value-type native code generation) and found none at all — the article makes no unsourced claim about it, which is the correct, cautious choice: 'the CLR keeps the real type around' (reification) and 'no boxing' (the benchmark) are both independently sourced/measured claims, and the article never conflates either with an unsourced statement about how the JIT compiles generic code for different type arguments.

Only one real finding, and it is a citation-precision nit, not a factual error: the sentence 'Variance is also restricted to interfaces and delegates in the first place — you cannot mark a type parameter of a class or struct as in or out' is cited to `csharp/programming-guide/concepts/covariance-contravariance/`, which only implies this restriction (it says variance is supported 'in generic interfaces and delegates', nothing about classes/structs being disallowed). The sentence that actually states the rule outright — 'Only interface types and delegate types can have variant type parameters' — is on `standard/generics/covariance-and-contravariance`, which is already in the source list and already cited two sentences earlier in the same paragraph for the IEnumerable/IComparer split. The fact itself is true and not in question; the citation just points at the weaker of the two sources that could support it.

No factual errors found anywhere after independently reproducing every diagnostic, both empirical claims, and every quoted source fragment.
